fields.apa_citation: Jahncke, H. (2012). Cognitive performance and restoration in open-plan office noise [Doctoral dissertation, University of Gavle and Lulea University of Technology]. ISBN 978-91-7439-495-5.
fields.main_conclusion: Open-plan office noise degrades word-memory performance and increases fatigue and motivational deficits, with the size of the impairment depending on which cognitive processes a task requires (tasks needing episodic memory and rehearsal are most vulnerable, and speech intelligibility above an STI of about 0.50 is especially harmful) and on individual hearing status, while a subsequent break filled with pleasant nature sound and imagery restores energy and motivation better than continued office noise.
independent_variables: Office background sound level (39 vs. 51 dB LAeq in Paper I; 30 vs. 60 dB LAeq in Paper II)
Hearing status (hearing-impaired vs. normal-hearing, Paper II)
Background speech intelligibility / Speech Transmission Index level (Paper III)
Presence vs. absence of irrelevant background speech (Paper IV)
Type of cognitive task (executive-function, memory, and fundamental office-task batteries)
Restoration/break condition (nature movie with sound, nature sound alone, silence, continued office noise)
dependent_variables: Response inhibition (SART, Flanker task) speed and accuracy
Serial recall, reading comprehension, arithmetic, and information-search performance
Self-rated fatigue and motivation (Swedish Occupational Fatigue Inventory)
fields.construct_pair: Open-plan office noise (sound level / speech intelligibility) -> Cognitive (working-memory) performance, self-rated fatigue, and restoration
fields.stimulus_description: In Paper I (the dissertation's first and most detailed study), 47 students worked for two hours in a simulated open-plan office exposed to recorded real office background noise (including phone rings and overheard telephone-style speech) played at either 39 or 51 dB(A) LAeq, then took a 7-minute break exposed to one of four conditions: a nature movie of a flowing river with matching sound, river sound alone, silence, or continued office noise.
fields.methods_surface_summary: A doctoral dissertation ('kappa') synthesizing four separate laboratory experiments: Paper I (n=47, mixed within/between-subjects design comparing 39 vs 51 dB LAeq office noise, analyzed with repeated-measures GLM/ANOVA) and Paper II (hearing-impaired vs. normal-hearing groups, 30 vs 60 dB LAeq) tested working-memory tasks, self-reported fatigue/motivation (SOFI), and salivary cortisol/urinary catecholamines, each followed by a restorative break; Paper III (n=42) tested cognitive performance across six graded levels of background-speech intelligibility (STI); Paper IV (n=24) tested performance with vs. without irrelevant background speech across tasks varying in semantic-processing demand.
measurement_inventory: Operation span and reading span tasks
Word generation (semantic and phonemic fluency) tasks

notes.main_conclusion: This dissertation reports four distinct studies (Papers I-IV). Per instructions to extract the paper's main/primary result, I treated Paper I -- the first-listed study, most fully detailed in the kappa, and foundational to the others -- as primary for sample_n, p_value, and effect_size, while main_conclusion synthesizes across all four papers as the dissertation's overall thesis.
notes.direction: Rated negative for the dissertation's dominant pattern (more/more-intelligible noise -> worse performance, more fatigue, less motivation), but this is not uniform: Paper II found normal-hearing participants unexpectedly performed BETTER in high vs. low noise on math and reading tasks (a positive/reversed direction for that subgroup), and several tasks in Papers I and IV showed no effect at all. The thesis authors themselves frame the overall pattern as negative but task- and person-dependent.
notes.sample_n: 47 students were recruited for Paper I; 9 were excluded for instruction non-compliance or equipment failure, leaving 38 for most analyses, and the key between-subjects noise-effect analysis on word memory used only the first-session data (n=18 low noise, n=20 high noise, total 38). Paper II used n=38 (20 hearing-impaired, 18 normal-hearing); Paper III used n=42; Paper IV used n=24.
notes.p_value: This is Paper I's principal reported result: the between-subjects main effect of noise condition on word-memory (proactive-interference) recall, F(1,30)=4.27, p<.05, partial eta-squared=0.13, reported as confirming the dissertation's Hypothesis 1.
notes.effect_size: Same result as p_value above (partial eta-squared=0.13). Other papers report their own effect estimates (e.g., a significant serial-recall difference between Paper I and Paper II normal-hearing groups, t(53)=2.27, p<.05) but no single common effect-size metric is used across all four papers.
notes.apa_citation: Front matter explicitly states author, title, degree, universities, and ISBN; no separate DOI or publisher name beyond 'Universitetstryckeriet, Lulea' (printer) is given.
